title: Make a roadside breakdown scene safer
summary: Protect people before diagnosing the vehicle. Stop as far from moving traffic as conditions safely allow and make the vehicle visible.
steps: Slow gradually, signal, and move completely off the travel lane if the vehicle can still be controlled.
Stop on firm, level ground. Apply the parking brake, select Park or a low gear, and turn on hazard lights.
Assess traffic, fire, fuel, weather, slope, and visibility before anyone exits.
If exiting is safer, use the side away from traffic and move behind a substantial barrier when available.
Place warning equipment only when doing so does not expose you to traffic.
Share your location, vehicle description, party condition, and direction of travel with help.
warnings: Never work in a live traffic lane.
If there is fire, smoke, a fuel smell, or a damaged high-voltage battery, move well away and contact emergency services.

source.title: Vehicle emergency and roadside safety guidance

title: Respond to an overheating engine
summary: An overheating warning can precede engine damage or a scalding-fluid release. Reduce load, stop safely, switch the engine off, and allow it to cool.
steps: Turn off air conditioning and reduce engine load while moving to a safe stopping place.
Stop, apply the parking brake, switch off the engine, and turn on hazard lights.
If there is steam, fire, or a fuel smell, keep away and use the fire-hazard procedure.
Wait until the engine is fully cool before any owner-manual inspection.
Check the vehicle owner's manual for the exact coolant reservoir and approved fluid.
Do not continue driving if the warning returns, coolant is leaking, or the cause is unknown.
warnings: Never open a hot radiator or pressurized cooling-system cap.
Do not pour cold water onto a hot engine.

source.title: Vehicle owner manual — cooling-system procedure required

title: Triage a vehicle that will not start
summary: Observe what happens when you attempt to start, but stop repeated attempts if there is smoke, a fuel smell, unusual heat, or mechanical impact noise.
steps: Confirm the transmission is in Park or Neutral, or the clutch is fully pressed, and apply the parking brake.
Note whether the dash is dark, lights are dim, there is a click, the engine cranks, or the engine starts then stops.
Turn off lights and accessories, wait one minute, and make one controlled start attempt.
Check the owner's manual for immobilizer, key-battery, jump-start, hybrid, or EV-specific instructions.
Only jump-start if the exact vehicle manual permits it and you have compatible equipment and a competent helper.
If the engine cranks but does not start, avoid draining the battery with repeated attempts.
warnings: Do not jump-start a frozen, leaking, swollen, damaged, or unidentified battery.
Never touch orange high-voltage cables or EV/hybrid traction components.

source.title: Vehicle owner manual — starting and jump-start procedure required

title: Decide whether a roadside tire change is safe
summary: A tire change is only appropriate on firm, level ground well outside traffic, using the vehicle's specified lift points and equipment.
steps: Move completely away from traffic to firm, level ground; use hazard lights and apply the parking brake.
Keep occupants away from traffic and assess wind, slope, soft ground, darkness, and passing-vehicle clearance.
Read the vehicle-specific jacking and spare-tire procedure before lifting.
If any safety condition is not met, do not lift the vehicle; request roadside help or move to a safer plan.
Never place any part of your body under a vehicle supported only by a jack.
After fitting a temporary spare, follow its speed, distance, and pressure limits.
warnings: Do not change a tire beside fast traffic, on a slope, or on unstable ground.
EV and hybrid lift points can be close to high-voltage battery structures; use only the marked points.

source.title: Vehicle owner manual — jacking and spare-tire procedure required

title: Make backcountry water safer
summary: Clear-looking natural water can contain disease-causing organisms. Prefer a known safe supply; otherwise collect from the best available source and treat it.
steps: Prefer moving water upstream from camps, livestock, mining, roads, and obvious contamination.
Let cloudy water settle and prefilter it through clean cloth before the main treatment.
Use a treatment method and contact time stated by its manufacturer.
When boiling is the available method, bring clear water to a rolling boil for 1 minute, or for 3 minutes above 6,500 feet (about 1,980 metres), then let it cool.
Store treated water in a clean, covered container and avoid recontaminating the cap or opening.
Ration physical effort and shade, not drinking water, when dehydration is a risk.
warnings: Cloth prefiltering removes sediment only; it does not make water microbiologically safe.
Boiling and common filters do not reliably remove fuels, heavy metals, salts, or toxic chemicals.
Do not drink seawater, urine, radiator fluid, or alcohol for hydration.

source.title: Water treatment while hiking, camping, and traveling
source.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

title: Stop and stabilize when lost
summary: Continuing without a reliable bearing often expands the search area. Stop, reduce immediate risks, make yourself findable, and move only for a clear safety reason.
steps: Stop. Breathe slowly, check injuries, and account for everyone.
Use Emergency SOS or a satellite communicator early if there is danger or an overdue plan.
Record your current location, time, battery, weather, and last known point.
If your present location is safe, stay together and avoid unplanned movement.
Make yourself visible with bright material, light, sound, and a clear ground signal when safe.
Prioritize shelter from the most immediate environmental threat, then water and a signaling plan.
warnings: Do not descend an unknown drainage, cross dangerous water, or take a 'shortcut' without a verified route.
Preserve phone power: lower brightness, use Low Power Mode, and transmit location deliberately.

source.title: Trip planning and backcountry safety guidance

title: Reduce cold exposure and hypothermia risk
summary: Wind, wet clothing, exhaustion, and cold ground can cause dangerous heat loss even above freezing.
steps: Move out of wind and precipitation; insulate the person from the ground.
Replace wet clothing with dry layers if this can be done without further exposure.
Warm the trunk gradually with dry insulation and shared body warmth.
If the person is alert and can swallow normally, offer warm non-alcoholic drinks.
Handle a severely cold, confused, or drowsy person gently and arrange evacuation.
Use Emergency SOS for altered mental state, slurred speech, loss of coordination, or reduced responsiveness.
warnings: Do not use alcohol, aggressive rubbing, or intense direct heat on a severely cold person.
Do not give drinks to someone who is drowsy, vomiting, or cannot swallow safely.

title: Control external bleeding
summary: Use firm, continuous direct pressure and arrange professional help for bleeding that is heavy or does not stop.
steps: Check scene safety and use gloves or a barrier when available.
Expose the wound enough to locate the bleeding without removing embedded objects.
Apply firm, continuous direct pressure with gauze or clean cloth.
If blood soaks through, add more material while maintaining pressure.
Use Emergency SOS for severe bleeding, shock signs, an embedded object, or a wound to the neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, or groin.
Keep the person warm, still, and observed until help takes over.
warnings: Do not remove embedded objects.
Tourniquets require appropriate equipment and current training; follow emergency-dispatcher or certified-course instructions.

title: Build and extinguish a campfire safely
summary: Use a fire only where local rules and current conditions allow it. Keep it small, attended, and fully extinguished before you leave or sleep.
steps: Check current fire restrictions, wind, and site rules before producing any flame.
Use an established fire ring when available and clear nearby dry fuel, overhanging branches, and flammable gear.
Keep water and a tool ready, add only small amounts of fuel, and never leave the fire unattended.
To extinguish, add water, stir the coals, add more water, and repeat until every part is cool to the touch.
If water is unavailable, thoroughly mix mineral soil or sand into spread-out embers; do not simply cover or bury hot coals.
warnings: Do not light a fire during a ban, in strong wind, or where escaping embers could ignite vegetation.
Never use gasoline or another volatile liquid to start or revive a campfire.

title: Choose a safer emergency shelter site
summary: A useful shelter reduces wind, rain, cold-ground, sun, or precipitation exposure without adding hazards from flooding, lightning, falling branches, cliffs, or fire.
steps: Identify the environmental threat that will harm you first, then choose shelter for that threat.
Prefer level, durable ground that is not the lowest point and is away from ravines, drainage channels, cliffs, and rising water.
Look up and around for dead trees, hanging branches, unstable rocks, steep slopes, and other fall hazards.
Insulate your body from the ground and block wind while keeping wet materials away from dry layers.
Keep the sleeping area safely separated from fire, cooking, food, garbage, and scented items.
warnings: A tent, tarp, picnic shelter, or isolated tree does not make an outdoor location safe from lightning.
Do not shelter in a dry drainage, flood channel, under dead limbs, or at the edge of a cliff.

source.title: Finding and Setting Up a Campsite

title: Protect food and keep wildlife out of camp
summary: Carried food is more dependable than improvised foraging. Secure every scented item, keep a clean camp, and follow the exact storage rules for the area.
steps: Check local requirements for lockers, approved bear-resistant containers, vehicles, or food hangs before the trip.
Secure food, garbage, cookware, toiletries, and every scented item whenever they are not in immediate use.
Prepare and eat away from the sleeping area where backcountry rules require separation.
Clean spills and cookware promptly, seal crumbs and waste, and pack out all food scraps and packaging.
Prefer compact carried food that tolerates the expected temperature; use foods requiring refrigeration first.
warnings: Never store food or scented items in a tent and never feed wildlife.
Do not eat an unknown plant, mushroom, berry, or animal based only on an app, photo, or short description.

title: Recognize heat exhaustion and heat stroke
summary: Heat illness can worsen quickly. Stop exertion, move to a cooler place, and treat confusion, loss of consciousness, or very hot skin as an emergency.
steps: Stop activity, move out of the heat, loosen excess clothing, and begin active cooling.
For a person who is alert and can swallow normally, offer small amounts of cool water while observing them.
Use cool wet cloths, airflow, or a cool bath when available and do not leave the person alone.
Use Emergency SOS immediately for confusion, seizure, collapse, loss of consciousness, or suspected heat stroke.
Continue rapid cooling while emergency help is being arranged.
warnings: Do not give anything to drink to a confused, unconscious, vomiting, or unsafe-to-swallow person.
Do not resume exertion while symptoms remain or are worsening.

source.title: First Aid for Heat Illness
source.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention / NIOSH

title: Reduce lightning exposure
summary: No outdoor location is safe during a thunderstorm. At the first thunder, reach a substantial enclosed building or a hard-topped vehicle when possible.
steps: At the first thunder or visible nearby lightning, stop the activity and move toward a substantial enclosed building or hard-topped vehicle.
Leave peaks, ridgelines, open fields, water, and isolated tall objects without delay.
Do not use a tent, open shelter, shallow overhang, or isolated tree as lightning protection.
If no safe place is reachable, spread the group apart and reduce exposure while continuing toward safer terrain.
Wait at least 30 minutes after the last thunder before returning outdoors.
warnings: There is no completely safe outdoor fallback during lightning.
Do not remain on or in water, on an exposed high point, or beneath an isolated tree.

title: Make yourself easier to find
summary: Call for help early when needed, transmit a precise location, then use deliberate visual and audible signals while avoiding movement that expands the search area.
steps: Use Emergency SOS, 911, or a satellite communicator early when there is immediate danger or an overdue trip plan.
Share coordinates when available, last known point, route, time, party condition, clothing, and visible landmarks.
If the location is safe, stay put and make a bright, high-contrast signal visible from more than one direction.
Use a whistle, light, or signal mirror in deliberate repeated groups rather than exhausting yourself with continuous noise.
Preserve phone power, keep communication devices warm and dry, and agree on scheduled check times.
warnings: Move from a known location only for an immediate threat or a clearly safer verified route.
Do not depend on a single signaling device or assume a sent message was received.

source.title: Outdoor Emergency Plan: If You Get Lost

title: Cool a thermal burn and identify emergency signs
summary: Stop the burning process, cool a thermal burn promptly with clean cool running water when available, and obtain urgent help for serious locations, sizes, or causes.
steps: Make the scene safe and stop contact with the heat source without exposing yourself.
Remove clothing or jewelry near the burn only when it is not stuck to skin.
Cool the area with clean, cool running water; use a clean cool compress if running water is unavailable.
Loosely protect the cooled burn with a clean non-adhesive dressing and monitor the person.
Use Emergency SOS for deep, large, electrical, chemical, explosive, airway, face, hand, foot, major-joint, or groin burns.
warnings: Do not use ice, butter, grease, ointment, or an adhesive bandage on a fresh burn.
Do not remove stuck material, break blisters, or attempt to clean a severe burn.

source.title: Burns: Types, Symptoms, and How To Help
